title: Chi-squared distribution
summary: A chi-squared random variable with k degrees of freedom is a sum of squares of k independent standard normals. Its mean is k and its variance is 2k. For normal samples, (n-1) times the sample variance over σ squared follows chi-squared with n-1 degrees of freedom.
intuition:
A chi-squared random variable is a sum of squares. Take $k$ independent standard normal variables and add their squares. The sum has the chi-squared distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom. The mean of that sum is $k$, one for each square, because a standard normal has second moment 1. The variance is $2k$. Both formulas are linear in the degrees of freedom, and the variance grows twice as fast as the mean.

The same family appears as the exact sampling law of a normal sample's variance. If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are i.i.d. normal with variance $\sigma^2$, and $s^2$ is the sample variance with divisor $n-1$, then

$$
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

The divisor $n-1$ is the sample-variance divisor. With that definition, $(n-1)s^2$ equals the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean, and dividing by $\sigma^2$ produces chi-squared with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. One degree of freedom is lost to estimating the mean. This exact statement needs normal data. Finite variance alone is not enough.

This object is not the chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic. That statistic is a function of observed and expected counts, and it is only approximately chi-squared when the counts are not tiny. The two lessons share a name because the test compares its statistic with a chi-squared reference distribution. The distribution in this lesson is the exact law of a sum of normal squares, and of the scaled sample variance.

definitions.term: Chi-squared with k degrees of freedom
definitions.body: The distribution of $Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_k^2$ when the $Z_i$ are i.i.d. standard normal. The degrees of freedom are $k$.
A chi-squared random variable with $k$ degrees of freedom has mean $k$ and variance $2k$.
For i.i.d. normal data, with $s^2$ the sample variance using divisor $n-1$, the ratio $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-squared with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

The goodness-of-fit statistic $\sum (O-E)^2/E$ is a different function, of counts. Under a null it is approximately chi-squared for large expected counts. It is not itself the sum of squares of standard normals.

formulas.name: Normal sample variance
formulas.note: Requires i.i.d. normal data. Here $s^2$ divides by $n-1$, so $(n-1)s^2=\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2$.

properties: The chi-squared distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom is the law of the sum of squares of $k$ independent standard normals. The mean is $k$ and the variance is $2k$.
For i.i.d. normal observations, $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$, where $s^2$ uses the sample divisor $n-1$.
The identity $(n-1)s^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2$ is the reason the degrees of freedom are $n-1$ rather than $n$. Estimating the mean costs one degree of freedom.
The exact chi-squared law for the sample variance needs normal data. It is not claimed for every i.i.d. sample with a finite variance.

The chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic is related only through its reference distribution. It is a function of counts, approximately chi-squared under the null, and it is not the same object as $Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_k^2$.

examples.title: Four standard normals
examples.prompt: Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_4$ be i.i.d. standard normal, and let $W=Z_1^2+Z_2^2+Z_3^2+Z_4^2$. Find the distribution, the mean, and the variance of $W$.
steps: A sum of squares of 4 independent standard normals is chi-squared with 4 degrees of freedom.
The mean is the degrees of freedom, so $\mathbb{E}[W]=4$.
The variance is twice the degrees of freedom, so $\mathrm{Var}(W)=8$.
examples.answer: The variable $W$ is chi-squared with 4 degrees of freedom, mean 4, and variance 8.

examples.title: Sample variance of eight normal observations
examples.prompt: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_8$ be i.i.d. normal with variance $\sigma^2$, and let $s^2$ be the sample variance with divisor $n-1$. Identify the distribution of $7s^2/\sigma^2$, and give its mean and variance.
steps: The sample size is $n=8$, so the degrees of freedom are $n-1=7$. The ratio $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2=7s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-squared with 7 degrees of freedom. This uses normality of the sample.
The sample variance divides by $7$, not by $8$. With that definition, $7s^2$ equals the sum of squared deviations from $\bar X$.

A chi-squared variable with 7 degrees of freedom has mean 7 and variance $2\times 7=14$. Those are properties of the reference distribution, not a claim that the observed value of $s^2$ equals $\sigma^2$.
examples.answer: The ratio $7s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-squared with 7 degrees of freedom. Its mean is 7 and its variance is 14.

traps: Using variance $k$ or $k^2$ instead of $2k$. The mean is $k$. The variance is $2k$.

Assigning $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ the degrees of freedom $n$, or using a population variance that divides by $n$ inside $s^2$ and still quoting $\chi^2_{n-1}$. The sample variance in this identity divides by $n-1$.
Claiming the exact chi-squared law for non-normal samples. The cheat-sheet identity needs i.i.d. normal data.

Identifying this distribution with the goodness-of-fit statistic $\sum (O-E)^2/E$. That statistic is compared with a chi-squared reference law. It is not the definition of the chi-squared distribution.
python:
assert 2 * 4 == 8
assert 8 - 1 == 7
assert 2 * 7 == 14
assert 2 * 6 == 12
assert 2 * 9 == 18
assert 12 - 1 == 11
print(8, 14, 9)

questions.stem: A chi-squared random variable has 6 degrees of freedom. Its variance is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $12$.

The variance is $2k=2\times 6=12$. Option B is the mean, which equals the degrees of freedom. Option C is $k^2$. Option D is $k/2$. The mean and the variance are different: 6 and 12.

questions.stem: For 12 i.i.d. normal observations, $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ follows a chi-squared distribution with how many degrees of freedom?
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $11$.

The exact sampling law for i.i.d. normal data uses $n-1=11$ degrees of freedom. The sample variance $s^2$ divides by $n-1$, and $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-squared with that same $n-1$. Option B forgets the degree of freedom lost to the sample mean. The result needs normality; it is not a general fact about every sample of size 12.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of the chi-squared distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom?
options: It is the distribution of the sum of squares of $k$ i.i.d. standard normals.
Every goodness-of-fit statistic $\sum (O-E)^2/E$ is exactly a sum of squares of standard normals, for any sample size.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The distribution is defined by that sum of squares, with mean $k$ and variance $2k$. Option D confuses the distribution with the count statistic from the test lesson. That statistic is only approximately chi-squared, and only under its null when expected counts are not tiny. It is not constructed as $Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_k^2$.

questions.stem: The variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are i.i.d. normal with variance $\sigma^2$, and $s^2$ is the sample variance with divisor $n-1$. Which of the following are true?
options: The ratio $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is chi-squared with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
The numerator identity $(n-1)s^2=\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2$ uses the $n-1$ divisor inside $s^2$.
The same exact chi-squared law holds for i.i.d. samples from every distribution with finite variance.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

For i.i.d. normal data the scaled sample variance is chi-squared with $n-1$ degrees of freedom, hence has mean $n-1$. The factor $n-1$ matches the sample-variance definition, so it converts $s^2$ into the sum of squared deviations. Option D drops the normality assumption. Finite variance is not enough for this exact law.

questions.stem: A chi-squared random variable has variance 18. Enter its degrees of freedom.
questions.solution:
The answer is **9**.

The variance is $2k=18$, so $k=9$. The mean is then also 9. Halving the variance recovers the degrees of freedom; using $k=18$ would confuse the variance with the mean.
